Home Editors Pick Agentic AI Google AI Releases Elephant-Goldfish Model Plugin for Spec-First Coding [...] Google has open-sourced the Elephant-Goldfish Model (EGM) plugin, a design-and-review layer for AI coding agents. The Elephant-Goldfish Model plugin makes an agent write a specification before it writes code. Fresh subagents with no conversation history then attack that spec. Google says thousands of its engineers use it. It is quite simple: catch wrong assumptions in a Markdown file, not in a pull request.

Those attempts followed September attacks that chained two SMA1000 zero-days to achieve remote code execution, as well as July attacks that exploited two other zero-days to deploy malware on vulnerable appliances. [...] # SonicWall warns of new SSL-VPN MFA bypass flaw exploited in attacks

SonicWall has released security updates to fix seven vulnerabilities in SonicOS firewalls, including an SSL-VPN authentication bypass flaw exploited in attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-19868, allows attackers with valid credentials for an alternate authentication method to bypass SAML authentication controls, potentially including SAML-enforced multi-factor authentication (MFA). [...] While SonicWall has not shared details about the reported exploitation, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has added CVE-2026-19868 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, confirming that the flaw has been exploited in the wild.

CISA ordered federal civilian executive branch agencies to secure affected systems by November 20, 2026.

title: Microsoft Paint flaw allows remote code execution | Cybernews
body:
Microsoft was forced to address a vulnerability in Microsoft Paint, titled CVE-2026-83844, that allows unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code remotely.

The vulnerability was put in the high-severity category with a score of 8.1 8.1 CVSS 3.1. Despite this, Microsoft had classed it as "important," which felt a few shades less serious. [...] Additionally, the flaw was classified as a CWE-125, known as an out-of-bounds read, meaning software accesses memory outside the boundaries of a buffer.

For example, if a program were told to read boxes 1-10, the malicious error exposed potentially sensitive errors in box 11, which could contain sensitive information.

title: OpenAI Jalapeño AI chip challenges Nvidia in inference
body:
Nvidia's near-monopoly over the most advanced AI chips is under "threat" as OpenAI's and other tech giants announce custom-built semiconductors, analysts told CNBC.

OpenAI announced that its first AI chip, the Jalapeño, had "industry-leading speed and efficiency," as it unveiled the semiconductor on Tuesday. Google, AWS and Meta are all also developing their own AI chips. [...] Nvidia has been approached for comment.

OpenAI announced the first benchmarking results from its Jalapeño, saying it would allow users to get "faster responses, more responsive agents and more reliable access" as demand grows.

The new chip is being developed with Broadcom. It will be deployed within OpenAI's compute infrastructure by the end of the year, and OpenAI said it was already working on the semiconductor's generations two and three. [...] The Jalapeño chip, designed for inference, shows that a "hyperscaler-designed chip can now match or beat Nvidia's Blackwell-class GPUs on inference efficiency," Adrien Sanchez, technology analyst at Yole Group, told CNBC.

He added that, while Nvidia still owns the "vast majority" of AI compute and has ecosystem lock-in to its software platform CUDA, OpenAI's new chip is a "threat to Nvidia's inference margins, which is the field growing the most at the moment."

# DOD expands its classified AI work with 8 companies — excluding Anthropic — amid ongoing dispute

DOD announced new agreements with SpaceX, OpenAI, Google, NVIDIA, Reflection, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, and Oracle.

By Brandi Vincent

Listen to this article

0:00 [...] DOD’s new deals with SpaceX, OpenAI, Google, NVIDIA, Reflection, Microsoft, Amazon Web Services, and Oracle follow a major contract dispute between the department and Anthropic that culminated earlier this year over potential ethical constraints that accompany the use of AI in warfare and for national surveillance. [...] Prior to CSET, Kahn was a policy advisor for force development and emerging capabilities in the Office of the Undersecretary of Defense for Policy at DOD.

In her view, the announcement “smartly highlights upfront” that these systems will be used for “lawful operational use,” thus acknowledging some of the anxieties circulating about frontier AI in the wake of the recent events.

title: Hiding in Plain Sight: The Geopolitics of Software Supply Chains
body: Companies frequently disclose risks such as export controls affecting technology products, political instability in regions where suppliers operate, or trade tensions that could have direct applications to industries in the defense, telecommunications, or the semiconductors space. For example, U.S. semiconductor export controls targeting advanced AI chips and semiconductor manufacturing equipment have been discussed as a source of supply chain disruption and geopolitical risk for technology [...] Defense acquisition policy in the United States has increasingly recognized supply chain risk through legislative and regulatory frameworks such as the National Defense Authorization Act (see Title VIII, Subtitle H—Other Matters) and Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (see Section 252.239-7018 Supply Chain Risk). The latter’s supply chain provisions allow the Pentagon to restrict the use of technologies that may present national security risks. The fact of possible foreign [...] Identifying and disclosing software supply chain risk is critical to mitigation efforts, yet current disclosure and compliance frameworks may only be capturing part of the risk. Discussions of geopolitical supply chain risk have traditionally centered on physical technologies such as semiconductors, telecommunications infrastructure, and critical manufacturing dependencies, while software ecosystems often remain comparatively invisible within broader strategic risk discussions. title: Pax Silica: alliances, frontier and markets in the geopolitics of the chip
body: Pax Silica is a non-binding declaration of intent. It should be read mainly as a signal to the rest of the world, since it introduces no new semiconductor policies but rather gives an epic, ‘Trump-style’ framing to what was already under way. Emilio García, in his weekly newsletter Chips y Poder, describes it as a solemn opening of a silicon curtain, with the US asserting its role as global regulator of the supply chain on one side of that divide. [...] It may seem that Trump’s more transactional doctrine, compared with Biden’s approach of controlling the diffusion of technology, is more compatible with middle powers that seek to maintain good relations with both US and Chinese technology. However, Pax Silica shows that this equidistance is possible only as long as it does not put the security of critical technology supply chains at risk, and it remains largely subject to US discretion. [...] Across this chain there are more than 50 points where a single region controls over 65% of the global market. With such a distributed architecture, the supply chain is highly exposed to political and geographic risks.
